```{r setup, include=FALSE}
if (!exists("params", inherits = FALSE)) {
  params <- list(
    data_file = "data/global_startup_success_dataset-selected-columns.csv",
    seed = 2026
  )
}

knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE, error = FALSE,
  fig.width = 9, fig.height = 5.5, dpi = 120
)

library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(glmnet)
library(recipes)
library(scales)
library(broom)

launch_palette <- list(
  violet = "#310A31",
  mauve = "#847996",
  teal = "#88B7B5",
  sage = "#A7CAB1",
  cream = "#F4ECD6",
  background = "#17111F",
  surface = "#21182C",
  grid = "#44384F"
)

theme_set(
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12, base_family = "sans") +
    theme(
      plot.title.position = "plot",
      plot.background = element_rect(fill = launch_palette$surface, color = NA),
      panel.background = element_rect(fill = launch_palette$surface, color = NA),
      panel.grid.major = element_line(color = launch_palette$grid, linewidth = 0.35),
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      plot.title = element_text(color = launch_palette$cream, face = "bold", size = 15),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(color = launch_palette$sage),
      axis.title = element_text(color = launch_palette$cream),
      axis.text = element_text(color = launch_palette$cream),
      strip.background = element_rect(fill = launch_palette$violet, color = NA),
      strip.text = element_text(color = launch_palette$cream, face = "bold"),
      legend.position = "bottom",
      legend.background = element_rect(fill = launch_palette$surface, color = NA),
      legend.key = element_rect(fill = launch_palette$surface, color = NA),
      legend.text = element_text(color = launch_palette$cream),
      legend.title = element_text(color = launch_palette$cream)
    )
)

required_columns <- c(
  "Startup Name", "Founded Year", "Country", "Industry", "Funding Stage",
  "Total Funding ($M)", "Number of Employees", "Annual Revenue ($M)",
  "Valuation ($B)", "Success Score"
)

raw <- read.csv(
  params$data_file,
  check.names = FALSE,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE,
  na.strings = c("", "NA", "N/A", "null")
)

# Treat whitespace-only cells as missing before checking for empty records.
raw[] <- lapply(raw, function(x) {
  if (is.character(x)) {
    x <- trimws(x)
    x[x == ""] <- NA_character_
  }
  x
})

missing_columns <- setdiff(required_columns, names(raw))
if (length(missing_columns) > 0) {
  stop("Missing required columns: ", paste(missing_columns, collapse = ", "))
}

input_rows <- nrow(raw)
# Remove rows that contain no information at all.
raw <- raw[rowSums(!is.na(raw)) > 0, , drop = FALSE]
has_data <- nrow(raw) > 0
```

## Startup roadmap

<p class="section-intro">A startup is not just a small company or a clever app. It is a team searching for a repeatable way to solve a meaningful problem—and a sustainable way to deliver that solution.</p>

<div class="card-grid three">
<article class="learning-card">
<span class="card-kicker">01 · Problem</span>
<h3>Find a real struggle</h3>
<p>Start with a specific person, a repeated frustration, and the cost of leaving it unsolved.</p>
</article>
<article class="learning-card">
<span class="card-kicker">02 · Evidence</span>
<h3>Replace guesses with learning</h3>
<p>Talk to people, study current workarounds, and look for behavior—not polite compliments.</p>
</article>
<article class="learning-card">
<span class="card-kicker">03 · Experiment</span>
<h3>Test the smallest promise</h3>
<p>Use a prototype, landing page, pilot, or manual service before building the full product.</p>
</article>
</div>

<div class="journey">
<button class="journey-step active" type="button" data-journey="problem"><span>1</span><strong>Problem</strong><small>Who struggles, and why?</small></button>
<button class="journey-step" type="button" data-journey="insight"><span>2</span><strong>Insight</strong><small>What does evidence reveal?</small></button>
<button class="journey-step" type="button" data-journey="solution"><span>3</span><strong>Solution</strong><small>What is your smallest promise?</small></button>
<button class="journey-step" type="button" data-journey="validation"><span>4</span><strong>Validation</strong><small>Will people act or pay?</small></button>
<button class="journey-step" type="button" data-journey="launch"><span>5</span><strong>Launch</strong><small>Can you deliver reliably?</small></button>
<button class="journey-step" type="button" data-journey="learn"><span>6</span><strong>Learn</strong><small>What should change next?</small></button>
</div>
<div class="journey-detail" id="journey-detail" aria-live="polite"><span>Right now</span><strong>Write down one repeated problem you have personally observed.</strong><p>Do not choose a solution yet. Name the person, moment, workaround, and cost.</p></div>

<div class="academy-content">
<div class="academy-topic-tabs" id="academy-topic-tabs" aria-label="Topics in this learning track"></div>
<section class="academy-panel active" data-academy-panel="foundation">
<div class="track-heading"><span>Track 01</span><h3>Turn an observation into a clear business idea</h3><p>Define the problem, the person, and the value before choosing features.</p></div>

<details class="academy-lesson" data-lesson="problem-statement" open>
<summary><span><small>Lesson 01</small>Problem statement</span><b>+</b></summary>
<div class="lesson-body">
<p>A useful problem statement names a specific customer, a situation, the job they are trying to do, the obstacle, and the cost of the problem. It should describe the problem without quietly prescribing your favorite solution.</p>
<div class="lesson-template"><strong>Template</strong><p><em>[Customer]</em> struggles to <em>[make progress]</em> when <em>[situation]</em> because <em>[root cause]</em>, causing <em>[time, money, risk, or frustration]</em>.</p></div>
<ul><li>Weak: “Students need a better food app.”</li><li>Stronger: “Students with evening labs struggle to find an affordable campus meal after 8 p.m., leading them to skip dinner or pay delivery fees.”</li></ul>
<button class="lesson-complete" type="button" data-complete-lesson="problem-statement">Mark lesson complete</button>
</div>
</details>

<details class="academy-lesson" data-lesson="customer-segment">
<summary><span><small>Lesson 02</small>Customer segment and profile</span><b>+</b></summary>
<div class="lesson-body">
<p>A segment is a group whose needs, behavior, and buying situation are similar enough for one focused strategy. “Everyone” is not a usable first segment.</p>
<div class="concept-grid four">
<div><strong>Demographics</strong><p>Age, income, education, role, organization size, or life stage.</p></div>
<div><strong>Geographics</strong><p>Country, region, campus, neighborhood, climate, or remote/in-person context.</p></div>
<div><strong>Psychographics</strong><p>Values, motivations, identity, attitudes, priorities, and risk tolerance.</p></div>
<div><strong>Behavior</strong><p>Frequency, trigger, current workaround, purchase process, and willingness to switch.</p></div>
</div>
<div class="lesson-template"><strong>Customer profile</strong><p>Our early adopter is <em>[specific person]</em> who experiences <em>[trigger/problem]</em> <em>[frequency]</em>, currently uses <em>[alternative]</em>, and cares most about <em>[desired outcome]</em>.</p></div>
<button class="lesson-complete" type="button" data-complete-lesson="customer-segment">Mark lesson complete</button>
</div>
</details>

<details class="academy-lesson" data-lesson="target-market">
<summary><span><small>Lesson 03</small>Target market and beachhead</span><b>+</b></summary>
<div class="lesson-body">
<p>Your target market is the segment you intentionally serve. Your beachhead is the smallest group you can reach, satisfy, and learn from first. Prioritize segments by problem intensity, reachability, ability to pay, urgency, and strategic fit.</p>
<div class="lesson-template"><strong>Decision test</strong><p>If you had only two weeks and $100, which customer group could you contact directly and offer a credible test to?</p></div>
<button class="lesson-complete" type="button" data-complete-lesson="target-market">Mark lesson complete</button>
</div>
</details>

<details class="academy-lesson" data-lesson="uvp">
<summary><span><small>Lesson 04</small>Unique value proposition (UVP)</span><b>+</b></summary>
<div class="lesson-body">
<p>A UVP explains the important outcome, the intended customer, and why your approach is meaningfully better than the current alternative. It is not a slogan.</p>
<div class="lesson-template"><strong>UVP statement</strong><p>For <em>[target customer]</em> who needs <em>[job/outcome]</em>, <em>[product]</em> is a <em>[category]</em> that <em>[primary benefit]</em>. Unlike <em>[alternative]</em>, it <em>[credible difference]</em>.</p></div>
<p><strong>Sustainable goals:</strong> decide whether environmental or social impact is part of the customer value, an operating constraint, or a measurable mission. Name the metric—such as waste avoided, access improved, or emissions reduced—rather than using vague “green” claims.</p>
<button class="lesson-complete" type="button" data-complete-lesson="uvp">Mark lesson complete</button>
</div>
</details>

<details class="academy-lesson" data-lesson="pitch">
<summary><span><small>Lesson 05</small>Elevator pitch</span><b>+</b></summary>
<div class="lesson-body">
<p>A strong 30–60 second pitch creates interest, not information overload. Lead with the customer and problem, explain the outcome, show one reason to believe, and end with a specific ask.</p>
<ol><li><strong>Hook:</strong> a concrete problem or surprising observation.</li><li><strong>Who + problem:</strong> the target user and costly moment.</li><li><strong>Solution + benefit:</strong> what changes for them.</li><li><strong>Proof:</strong> interviews, pilot results, traction, or relevant insight.</li><li><strong>Ask:</strong> an introduction, interview, pilot, feedback, or funding conversation.</li></ol>
<button class="lesson-complete" type="button" data-complete-lesson="pitch">Mark lesson complete</button>
</div>
</details>

<div class="workbench pitch-workbench" data-tool-for="pitch">
<div class="workbench-heading"><span>Interactive tool</span><h3>Build your elevator pitch</h3><p>Fill in the pieces and Nessie will assemble a first draft.</p></div>
<div class="workbench-fields">
<label>Target customer<input class="pitch-input" id="pitch-customer" placeholder="First-year commuter students"></label>
<label>Problem<input class="pitch-input" id="pitch-problem" placeholder="miss useful campus events"></label>
<label>Solution<input class="pitch-input" id="pitch-solution" placeholder="a personalized event digest"></label>
<label>Primary benefit<input class="pitch-input" id="pitch-benefit" placeholder="find relevant events in under a minute"></label>
<label>Difference or proof<input class="pitch-input" id="pitch-proof" placeholder="built from 20 student interviews"></label>
<label>Your ask<input class="pitch-input" id="pitch-ask" placeholder="five students for a one-week pilot"></label>
</div>
<div class="workbench-output">
<span>Pitch draft</span>
<p id="pitch-output">Complete the fields to build a clear 30-second pitch.</p>
<div class="pitch-actions"><button id="generate-pitch" type="button">Generate my pitch</button><button id="copy-pitch" type="button">Copy pitch</button></div>
</div>
</div>
</section>

<section class="academy-panel" data-academy-panel="validation" hidden>
<div class="track-heading"><span>Track 02</span><h3>Test behavior before building too much</h3><p>Use interviews and small experiments to replace opinions with evidence.</p></div>

<details class="academy-lesson" data-lesson="features-benefits" open>
<summary><span><small>Lesson 06</small>Features and benefits</span><b>+</b></summary>
<div class="lesson-body">
<p>A feature is what the product does. A benefit is the useful change a customer experiences. Connect every feature to the problem, outcome, and evidence needed.</p>
<div class="mini-table"><div><strong>Feature</strong><strong>Benefit</strong><strong>Proof metric</strong></div><div><span>One-click event filter</span><span>Less searching</span><span>Time to find an event</span></div><div><span>Deadline reminders</span><span>Fewer missed tasks</span><span>On-time completion rate</span></div></div>
<p>Prioritize with <strong>must-have, should-have, could-have, not-now</strong>. A top feature directly solves the primary problem; an impressive feature that does not is still a distraction.</p>
<button class="lesson-complete" type="button" data-complete-lesson="features-benefits">Mark lesson complete</button>
</div>
</details>

<details class="academy-lesson" data-lesson="mvp">
<summary><span><small>Lesson 07</small>Minimum viable product</span><b>+</b></summary>
<div class="lesson-body">
<p>An MVP is the smallest experience that tests your riskiest business assumption while still delivering enough value for a real response. It may be a landing page, concierge service, spreadsheet, preorder, clickable prototype, or limited pilot.</p>
<div class="lesson-template"><strong>MVP test</strong><p>We need to learn whether <em>[customer]</em> will <em>[meaningful behavior]</em> for <em>[outcome]</em>. We can test this with <em>[small experience]</em> and will continue if <em>[threshold]</em>.</p></div>
<button class="lesson-complete" type="button" data-complete-lesson="mvp">Mark lesson complete</button>
</div>
</details>

<details class="academy-lesson" data-lesson="customer-interviews">
<summary><span><small>Lesson 08</small>Customer interviews</span><b>+</b></summary>
<div class="lesson-body">
<p>Interview people who recently experienced the problem. Ask about specific past events, not imagined future behavior. Do not pitch during a problem interview.</p>
<ul><li>“Tell me about the last time this happened.”</li><li>“What did you do next?”</li><li>“What was hardest, slowest, or most expensive?”</li><li>“What have you already tried?”</li><li>“Who decides or pays?”</li></ul>
<p>Write exact quotes, behaviors, workarounds, frequency, and contradictions. Five interviews can reveal patterns; they do not prove an entire market.</p>
<button class="lesson-complete" type="button" data-complete-lesson="customer-interviews">Mark lesson complete</button>
</div>
</details>

<details class="academy-lesson" data-lesson="solution-interviews">
<summary><span><small>Lesson 09</small>Solution interviews and usability</span><b>+</b></summary>
<div class="lesson-body">
<p>After the problem is understood, show a low-fidelity solution. Give the participant a realistic task and ask them to think aloud. Watch where they hesitate instead of teaching them how it works.</p>
<p>End with a meaningful commitment: join a pilot, schedule a follow-up, share data, introduce a buyer, preorder, or pay. Compliments are not validation.</p>
<button class="lesson-complete" type="button" data-complete-lesson="solution-interviews">Mark lesson complete</button>
</div>
</details>

<details class="academy-lesson" data-lesson="experiments">
<summary><span><small>Lesson 10</small>Marketing tests and survey results</span><b>+</b></summary>
<div class="lesson-body">
<p>A useful experiment has one hypothesis, one audience, one offer, one primary metric, a time limit, and a decision rule set before launch. Examples include two landing-page messages, waitlist conversion, outreach replies, a small paid-ad test, or two price points.</p>
<p>Surveys are strongest for measuring patterns after interviews help you write good questions. Report sample source, sample size, question wording, response distribution, missing responses, and limitations. Avoid treating a convenience sample as the whole market.</p>
<button class="lesson-complete" type="button" data-complete-lesson="experiments">Mark lesson complete</button>
</div>
</details>
</section>

<section class="academy-panel" data-academy-panel="market" hidden>
<div class="track-heading"><span>Track 03</span><h3>Understand the market and the alternatives</h3><p>Size the opportunity, study competition, and test feasibility.</p></div>

<details class="academy-lesson" data-lesson="market-sizing" open>
<summary><span><small>Lesson 11</small>Market sizing: TAM, SAM, SOM</span><b>+</b></summary>
<div class="lesson-body">
<div class="concept-grid three"><div><strong>TAM</strong><p>Total annual demand if every relevant buyer used your solution.</p></div><div><strong>SAM</strong><p>The portion you can serve with your product, geography, channel, and constraints.</p></div><div><strong>SOM</strong><p>The realistic share you could capture in a defined period with available resources.</p></div></div>
<p>Use both <strong>top-down</strong> sources and a <strong>bottom-up</strong> model: reachable accounts × realistic annual revenue per account. State every assumption and never present TAM as a sales forecast.</p>
<button class="lesson-complete" type="button" data-complete-lesson="market-sizing">Mark lesson complete</button>
</div>
</details>

<div class="workbench market-workbench" data-tool-for="market-sizing">
<div class="workbench-heading"><span>Interactive tool</span><h3>TAM → SAM → SOM calculator</h3><p>Build a transparent bottom-up estimate.</p></div>
<div class="workbench-fields compact">
<label>Potential customers<input id="market-customers" type="number" min="0" value="10000"></label>
<label>Annual revenue per customer (&#36;)<input id="market-arpc" type="number" min="0" value="120"></label>
<label>Serviceable share (%)<input id="market-sam-share" type="number" min="0" max="100" value="25"></label>
<label>Obtainable share of SAM (%)<input id="market-som-share" type="number" min="0" max="100" value="5"></label>
</div>
<div class="market-results"><div><span>TAM</span><strong id="tam-result">&#36;1,200,000</strong></div><div><span>SAM</span><strong id="sam-result">&#36;300,000</strong></div><div><span>SOM</span><strong id="som-result">&#36;15,000</strong></div></div>
</div>

<details class="academy-lesson" data-lesson="competition">
<summary><span><small>Lesson 12</small>Competitive analysis</span><b>+</b></summary>
<div class="lesson-body">
<p>Competition includes direct products, indirect approaches, do-it-yourself workarounds, and doing nothing. Compare the customer segment, job solved, pricing, channel, strengths, weaknesses, switching costs, and proof—not just feature counts.</p>
<p>Use the analysis to find an underserved need or a different tradeoff. “We have no competitors” usually means the current workaround has not been identified.</p>
<a class="lesson-source" href="https://www.sba.gov/business-guide/plan-your-business/market-research-competitive-analysis" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Official SBA market-research guide ↗</a>
<button class="lesson-complete" type="button" data-complete-lesson="competition">Mark lesson complete</button>
</div>
</details>

<details class="academy-lesson" data-lesson="swot">
<summary><span><small>Lesson 13</small>SWOT and feasibility</span><b>+</b></summary>
<div class="lesson-body">
<p><strong>Strengths and weaknesses</strong> are internal. <strong>Opportunities and threats</strong> are external. Convert the list into action: use a strength to pursue an opportunity, correct a weakness, and reduce exposure to a threat.</p>
<p>Feasibility asks whether the venture is desirable to customers, technically and operationally possible, legally responsible, and financially sustainable. Identify the assumption that could break the idea first.</p>
<button class="lesson-complete" type="button" data-complete-lesson="swot">Mark lesson complete</button>
</div>
</details>

<div class="workbench swot-workbench" data-tool-for="swot">
<div class="workbench-heading"><span>Interactive tool</span><h3>Build a one-page SWOT</h3><p>Keep each box specific and connected to evidence.</p></div>
<div class="swot-grid">
<label><span>Strengths</span><textarea class="swot-input" id="swot-strengths" rows="4" placeholder="Capabilities, access, proof…"></textarea></label>
<label><span>Weaknesses</span><textarea class="swot-input" id="swot-weaknesses" rows="4" placeholder="Gaps, constraints, unknowns…"></textarea></label>
<label><span>Opportunities</span><textarea class="swot-input" id="swot-opportunities" rows="4" placeholder="Trends, unmet needs, partnerships…"></textarea></label>
<label><span>Threats</span><textarea class="swot-input" id="swot-threats" rows="4" placeholder="Competitors, regulation, substitutes…"></textarea></label>
</div>
<small>Saved automatically in this browser.</small>
</div>
</section>

<section class="academy-panel" data-academy-panel="marketing" hidden>
<div class="track-heading"><span>Track 04</span><h3>Make the right promise in the right place</h3><p>Connect brand, channels, content, and a trustworthy website.</p></div>

<details class="academy-lesson" data-lesson="branding" open>
<summary><span><small>Lesson 14</small>Branding</span><b>+</b></summary>
<div class="lesson-body">
<p>A brand is the expectation people build from every interaction. Define your audience, positioning, personality, promise, reasons to believe, voice, visual system, and consistency rules. A logo supports the brand; it is not the whole brand.</p>
<p>Before committing to a name, check domain availability, social handles, state business records, and similar trademarks. Test whether the name is pronounceable, memorable, and appropriate across likely markets.</p>
<button class="lesson-complete" type="button" data-complete-lesson="branding">Mark lesson complete</button>
</div>
</details>

<details class="academy-lesson" data-lesson="marketing-plan">
<summary><span><small>Lesson 15</small>Marketing plan, mix, and functions</span><b>+</b></summary>
<div class="lesson-body">
<p>The classic marketing mix is <strong>Product, Price, Place, and Promotion</strong>. Services often add <strong>People, Process, and Physical evidence</strong>. Make the choices reinforce one position.</p>
<div class="concept-grid three"><div><strong>Research</strong><p>Segments, needs, competitors, trends, and demand.</p></div><div><strong>Offer</strong><p>Product design, benefits, brand, packaging, and pricing.</p></div><div><strong>Go to market</strong><p>Distribution, promotion, sales, service, and retention.</p></div></div>
<p>A one-page plan should name the objective, audience, insight, message, offer, channels, budget, calendar, owner, primary metric, and review date.</p>
<button class="lesson-complete" type="button" data-complete-lesson="marketing-plan">Mark lesson complete</button>
</div>
</details>

<details class="academy-lesson" data-lesson="social-advertising">
<summary><span><small>Lesson 16</small>Social media and advertising</span><b>+</b></summary>
<div class="lesson-body">
<p>Choose channels based on where the customer already pays attention and how they make the purchase—not which platform is newest. Build content around customer questions, useful proof, demonstrations, stories, and calls to action.</p>
<p>For paid tests, define audience, creative, offer, landing page, budget cap, and one conversion metric. Track impressions → clicks → qualified actions → customers. Advertising claims must be truthful, supported, and not misleading; disclose material connections with endorsers clearly.</p>
<a class="lesson-source" href="https://www.ftc.gov/business-guidance/advertising-marketing" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Official FTC advertising guidance ↗</a>
<button class="lesson-complete" type="button" data-complete-lesson="social-advertising">Mark lesson complete</button>
</div>
</details>

<details class="academy-lesson" data-lesson="website">
<summary><span><small>Lesson 17</small>Website and domain—from zero to launch</span><b>+</b></summary>
<div class="lesson-body">
<ol class="website-steps">
<li><strong>Choose the job:</strong> validation landing page, portfolio, booking site, store, community, or product app.</li>
<li><strong>Pick a name and domain:</strong> choose a short, readable domain through an accredited registrar. You rent registration by the year; enable auto-renew, account MFA, registrar lock, and accurate contact information.</li>
<li><strong>Choose a platform:</strong> a hosted builder is fastest; a CMS offers content flexibility; static HTML/GitHub Pages is inexpensive for informational sites; a web application needs hosting, a database, authentication, and maintenance.</li>
<li><strong>Connect DNS:</strong> the registrar manages ownership; DNS records point the domain to hosting. Common records include A/AAAA, CNAME, MX for email, and TXT for verification/security.</li>
<li><strong>Design the core journey:</strong> one clear audience, headline/UVP, benefits and proof, strong call to action, contact details, and only the pages users need.</li>
<li><strong>Make it trustworthy:</strong> HTTPS, mobile layout, accessible contrast and labels, fast images, working forms, privacy notice, terms when appropriate, refund/shipping policies for commerce, and truthful claims.</li>
<li><strong>Measure:</strong> analytics with consent where required, search-console verification, conversion events, uptime, and form testing. Collect only data you need.</li>
<li><strong>Maintain:</strong> renew domain and hosting, update software, back up content, patch security issues, test links/forms, and keep owner access documented.</li>
</ol>
<p><strong>Minimum pages:</strong> Home, Product/Service, About or credibility, Contact, and required policy pages. Add FAQ, pricing, case studies, or a blog only when they support a customer decision.</p>
<p><strong>SEO basics:</strong> useful page titles, one clear topic per page, descriptive URLs, headings that match questions, original helpful content, alt text, internal links, sitemap, and performance. SEO cannot rescue a page that gives visitors no value.</p>
<div class="source-row"><a class="lesson-source" href="https://www.icann.org/en/system/files/files/registering-domain-name-15feb23-en.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener">ICANN domain guide ↗</a><a class="lesson-source" href="https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/seo-starter-guide" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Google SEO starter guide ↗</a></div>
<button class="lesson-complete" type="button" data-complete-lesson="website">Mark lesson complete</button>
</div>
</details>

<div class="workbench website-workbench" data-tool-for="website">
<div class="workbench-heading"><span>Interactive checklist</span><h3>Website launch check</h3><p>Check items as you complete them; progress is saved locally.</p></div>
<div class="website-check-grid">
<label><input class="website-check" type="checkbox"> One audience and one primary action</label>
<label><input class="website-check" type="checkbox"> Domain owner, renewal, MFA, and recovery documented</label>
<label><input class="website-check" type="checkbox"> HTTPS and custom domain working</label>
<label><input class="website-check" type="checkbox"> Mobile, keyboard, contrast, and form labels tested</label>
<label><input class="website-check" type="checkbox"> Privacy, terms, contact, and commerce policies reviewed</label>
<label><input class="website-check" type="checkbox"> Analytics/conversions and search tools configured</label>
<label><input class="website-check" type="checkbox"> Forms, links, payments, email, and error pages tested</label>
<label><input class="website-check" type="checkbox"> Backups, updates, renewals, and ownership handoff planned</label>
</div>
<div class="website-check-result"><strong id="website-check-count">0/8 ready</strong><span id="website-check-note">Start with the site’s main job.</span></div>
</div>
</section>

<section class="academy-panel" data-academy-panel="money" hidden>
<div class="track-heading"><span>Track 05</span><h3>Build an economic model, not just a price</h3><p>Understand revenue, direct costs, cash, projections, and possible exits.</p></div>

<details class="academy-lesson" data-lesson="revenue-models" open>
<summary><span><small>Lesson 18</small>Revenue models</span><b>+</b></summary>
<div class="lesson-body">
<p>Common models include one-time sales, subscription, usage-based, transaction fee, marketplace commission, licensing, advertising, sponsorship, freemium, services, leasing, and franchising. Choose based on how value is delivered and how customers prefer to buy.</p>
<p>Test the unit: who pays, for what, how often, through which contract or checkout, and what causes expansion or cancellation. Mixing models too early makes learning harder.</p>
<button class="lesson-complete" type="button" data-complete-lesson="revenue-models">Mark lesson complete</button>
</div>
</details>

<details class="academy-lesson" data-lesson="cogs-pricing">
<summary><span><small>Lesson 19</small>COGS, margin, and pricing strategy</span><b>+</b></summary>
<div class="lesson-body">
<p><strong>COGS</strong> includes direct costs required to deliver one unit: materials, production labor, packaging, transaction fees, shipping subsidy, or usage-based infrastructure. Gross profit = revenue − COGS; gross margin % = gross profit ÷ revenue.</p>
<p>Pricing approaches include cost-plus, competitor-based, value-based, tiered, penetration, skimming, bundle, subscription, and usage-based. Use costs as a floor, customer value and alternatives as context, then test willingness to pay. Include discounts, returns, taxes, channel fees, and support in the model.</p>
<button class="lesson-complete" type="button" data-complete-lesson="cogs-pricing">Mark lesson complete</button>
</div>
</details>

<div class="workbench pricing-workbench" data-tool-for="cogs-pricing">
<div class="workbench-heading"><span>Interactive tool</span><h3>Price and unit-economics check</h3><p>See whether a price covers direct cost and contributes toward overhead.</p></div>
<div class="workbench-fields compact">
<label>Price per unit (&#36;)<input id="pricing-price" type="number" min="0" step="0.01" value="25"></label>
<label>Direct COGS per unit (&#36;)<input id="pricing-cogs" type="number" min="0" step="0.01" value="8"></label>
<label>Monthly fixed costs (&#36;)<input id="pricing-fixed" type="number" min="0" step="0.01" value="1000"></label>
<label>Expected monthly units<input id="pricing-units" type="number" min="0" step="1" value="100"></label>
<label>Closest competitor price (&#36;)<input id="pricing-competitor" type="number" min="0" step="0.01" value="24"></label>
<label>Estimated customer value ceiling (&#36;)<input id="pricing-value" type="number" min="0" step="0.01" value="35"></label>
</div>
<div class="pricing-strategies" aria-label="Pricing strategy scenarios">
<button class="pricing-strategy active" type="button" data-pricing-strategy="margin">Target margin</button>
<button class="pricing-strategy" type="button" data-pricing-strategy="cost">Cost-plus</button>
<button class="pricing-strategy" type="button" data-pricing-strategy="competition">Competition-led</button>
<button class="pricing-strategy" type="button" data-pricing-strategy="value">Value-based</button>
<button class="pricing-strategy" type="button" data-pricing-strategy="penetration">Penetration</button>
<button class="pricing-strategy" type="button" data-pricing-strategy="skimming">Skimming</button>
</div>
<div class="pricing-scenario" id="pricing-scenario"><span>Target-margin scenario</span><strong>Suggested starting point: &#36;20.00</strong><p>At &#36;8.00 COGS, a 60% target gross margin requires a &#36;20.00 price. Test whether customers perceive enough value at that price.</p></div>
<div class="market-results"><div><span>Current gross margin</span><strong id="margin-result">68.0%</strong></div><div><span>Monthly contribution</span><strong id="contribution-result">$1,700</strong></div><div><span>Break-even units</span><strong id="breakeven-result">59</strong></div></div>
</div>

<details class="academy-lesson" data-lesson="financial-model">
<summary><span><small>Lesson 20</small>Financial model and banking</span><b>+</b></summary>
<div class="lesson-body">
<p>A useful model connects assumptions to monthly revenue, COGS, payroll, operating expenses, cash flow, and cash balance. Build a base case plus conservative and upside scenarios. Track actuals against the model and update assumptions rather than hiding misses.</p>
<p>Core statements serve different jobs: the income statement shows performance over time, the cash-flow statement explains cash movement, and the balance sheet shows assets, liabilities, and equity at a point in time.</p>
<p>Before accepting or spending business money, choose the entity and tax setup, obtain required registrations/EIN, then compare business accounts by fees, transaction limits, deposit insurance, payment tools, integrations, and signer controls. Keep business and personal activity separate and reconcile monthly.</p>
<a class="lesson-source" href="https://www.irs.gov/publications/p583" target="_blank" rel="noopener">IRS starting and recordkeeping guidance ↗</a>
<button class="lesson-complete" type="button" data-complete-lesson="financial-model">Mark lesson complete</button>
</div>
</details>

<details class="academy-lesson" data-lesson="exit-strategy">
<summary><span><small>Lesson 21</small>Funding and exit strategies</span><b>+</b></summary>
<div class="lesson-body">
<p>Funding may come from revenue/bootstrapping, grants, competitions, friends and family, crowdfunding, debt, angels, venture capital, or strategic partners. Match the source to risk, repayment ability, growth expectations, ownership tradeoffs, and use of funds.</p>
<p>Possible exits include owner operation, family or employee succession, acquisition, merger, management buyout, licensing assets, public offering for rare high-growth firms, or orderly closure. Plan clean records, transferable contracts, documented IP, governance, and reduced dependence on one founder long before an exit.</p>
<a class="lesson-source" href="https://www.sba.gov/business-guide/manage-your-business/close-or-sell-your-business" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Official SBA exit guidance ↗</a>
<button class="lesson-complete" type="button" data-complete-lesson="exit-strategy">Mark lesson complete</button>
</div>
</details>
</section>

<section class="academy-panel" data-academy-panel="legal" hidden>
<div class="track-heading"><span>Track 06</span><h3>Protect the company, founders, customers, and work</h3><p>This U.S.-focused overview is a decision checklist—not personal legal or tax advice.</p></div>

<details class="academy-lesson" data-lesson="structures-partnerships" open>
<summary><span><small>Lesson 22</small>Structures, founders, and partnerships</span><b>+</b></summary>
<div class="lesson-body">
<p>Common U.S. forms include sole proprietorship, general or limited partnership, LLP, LLC, and corporation. The choice changes liability, taxes, governance, fundraising, filing, and administration. Rules vary by state and situation.</p>
<p>“Partnership” can also describe a working relationship: co-marketing, referral/affiliate, distribution, supplier, licensing, joint venture, strategic alliance, or equity partnership. Put scope, ownership, money, confidentiality, performance, brand use, liability, data, termination, and dispute terms in writing.</p>
<p>Founder agreements should address roles, decision rights, equity, vesting, IP assignment, time commitment, compensation, fundraising, departures, deadlock, and what happens if someone stops contributing.</p>
<a class="lesson-source" href="https://www.sba.gov/business-guide/launch-your-business/choose-business-structure" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Compare structures at SBA.gov ↗</a>
<button class="lesson-complete" type="button" data-complete-lesson="structures-partnerships">Mark lesson complete</button>
</div>
</details>

<details class="academy-lesson" data-lesson="ip-nda-attorney">
<summary><span><small>Lesson 23</small>Trademarks, patents, NDAs, and attorneys</span><b>+</b></summary>
<div class="lesson-body">
<div class="concept-grid four"><div><strong>Trademark</strong><p>Protects source-identifying names, logos, and related brand elements for goods/services.</p></div><div><strong>Patent</strong><p>May protect a qualifying new invention; it gives exclusion rights, not automatic permission to practice it.</p></div><div><strong>Copyright</strong><p>Protects original expression such as writing, art, code, photos, or video—not the underlying idea.</p></div><div><strong>Trade secret</strong><p>Protects valuable confidential information when reasonable secrecy measures are maintained.</p></div></div>
<p>Search before adopting a brand or filing. Patent timing can matter, and public disclosure may affect rights. NDAs can define confidential information, permitted use, exclusions, duration, return/destruction, and remedies, but they do not replace access controls, IP assignment, or a well-scoped contract.</p>
<p>Talk to an attorney when founder equity or ownership is unclear, a regulated product is involved, meaningful contracts or hiring begin, IP is core to the venture, investors are approaching, a dispute or demand arrives, or the cost of being wrong is high. For patents, consider a USPTO-registered patent attorney or agent.</p>
<div class="source-row"><a class="lesson-source" href="https://www.uspto.gov/trademarks/basics" target="_blank" rel="noopener">USPTO trademark basics ↗</a><a class="lesson-source" href="https://www.uspto.gov/patents/basics/essentials" target="_blank" rel="noopener">USPTO patent essentials ↗</a></div>
<button class="lesson-complete" type="button" data-complete-lesson="ip-nda-attorney">Mark lesson complete</button>
</div>
</details>

<div class="workbench trademark-workbench" data-tool-for="ip-nda-attorney">
<div class="workbench-heading"><span>Interactive pre-screen</span><h3>Check a possible brand name</h3><p>This tool helps you plan a clearance search. It cannot determine availability, ownership, registration, or likelihood of confusion.</p></div>
<div class="workbench-fields">
<label>Proposed name<input id="trademark-name" type="text" maxlength="80" placeholder="Example: Strictly Business"></label>
<label>Goods or services<input id="trademark-goods" type="text" maxlength="140" placeholder="Example: student startup education website"></label>
</div>
<button class="trademark-check-button" id="trademark-check" type="button">Run name pre-screen</button>
<div class="trademark-result" id="trademark-result" aria-live="polite">
<div><span>Preliminary signal</span><strong>Enter a name and what it identifies.</strong></div>
<p>The same or similar wording may coexist for unrelated goods, while different spellings can still conflict when sound, appearance, meaning, and commercial impression are similar.</p>
<ul id="trademark-checklist"><li>Exact wording and close variations</li><li>Similar sound, spelling, meaning, and translation</li><li>Related goods/services and trade channels</li><li>Federal, state, business-name, domain, and common-law sources</li></ul>
<div class="trademark-links">
<a id="trademark-uspto-link" href="https://www.uspto.gov/trademarks/search/search" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Search USPTO records ↗</a>
<a id="trademark-web-link" href="https://www.google.com/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Search the wider web ↗</a>
<a id="trademark-domain-link" href="https://lookup.icann.org/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Check domain registration ↗</a>
</div>
</div>
<p class="tool-disclaimer">A complete U.S. clearance search also considers inactive records, related goods/services, state records, business names, domains, and unregistered common-law use. Consider a U.S.-licensed trademark attorney before adopting or filing an important brand.</p>
</div>

<details class="academy-lesson" data-lesson="legal-operations">
<summary><span><small>Lesson 24</small>Legal and financial launch checklist</span><b>+</b></summary>
<div class="lesson-body">
<div class="legal-check-columns">
<div><strong>Form and register</strong><ul><li>Choose entity, state, business name, and ownership</li><li>Register assumed names where required</li><li>Obtain EIN/tax IDs and licenses/permits</li><li>Document governance and founder approvals</li></ul></div>
<div><strong>Operate responsibly</strong><ul><li>Separate bank account, bookkeeping, taxes, and records</li><li>Written customer, vendor, contractor, and employee terms</li><li>Insurance appropriate to product and risk</li><li>Privacy, cybersecurity, accessibility, and data retention</li></ul></div>
<div><strong>Protect assets</strong><ul><li>IP ownership and assignments from every contributor</li><li>Trademark/domain clearance and renewal calendar</li><li>Confidentiality and restricted access</li><li>Contract, compliance, and corporate-record storage</li></ul></div>
</div>
<p>Requirements depend on location, industry, workforce, customers, and data. Recheck federal, state, local, and industry rules before launch and as the business changes.</p>
<div class="source-row"><a class="lesson-source" href="https://www.sba.gov/business-guide/launch-your-business" target="_blank" rel="noopener">SBA launch checklist ↗</a><a class="lesson-source" href="https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/starting-a-business" target="_blank" rel="noopener">IRS starting-a-business guide ↗</a></div>
<button class="lesson-complete" type="button" data-complete-lesson="legal-operations">Mark lesson complete</button>
</div>
</details>
</section>

<section class="academy-panel" data-academy-panel="finish" hidden>
<div class="track-heading"><span>Track 07</span><h3>Turn the evidence into a decision</h3><p>Finish with a business case that makes assumptions and limitations visible.</p></div>
<div class="finish-grid">
<article><span>01</span><h3>Summary of key points</h3><p>Restate the customer, problem, UVP, solution, market, model, evidence, economics, risks, and next milestone in plain language.</p></article>
<article><span>02</span><h3>Feasibility</h3><p>Rate desirability, technical delivery, operations, legal responsibility, and financial viability. Name what still needs proof.</p></article>
<article><span>03</span><h3>SWOT</h3><p>Translate the four boxes into actions, owners, evidence, and review dates instead of ending with a list.</p></article>
<article><span>04</span><h3>Competitive analysis</h3><p>Explain the current alternatives, your focused advantage, switching barriers, and how competitors may respond.</p></article>
<article><span>05</span><h3>Survey and interview results</h3><p>Report method, sample, exact measures, findings, contradictions, bias, and what the evidence does—and does not—support.</p></article>
<article><span>06</span><h3>Conclusion and next test</h3><p>Choose continue, revise, pause, or stop. Define the next assumption, test, threshold, budget, owner, and decision date.</p></article>
</div>
<div class="lesson-template finish-template"><strong>Final recommendation</strong><p>Based on <em>[evidence]</em>, we recommend <em>[decision]</em> because <em>[reason]</em>. The largest remaining risk is <em>[assumption]</em>, which we will test by <em>[experiment]</em> before <em>[date]</em>.</p></div>
<a class="button primary" href="#problem-to-solution">Build your idea canvas</a>
<a class="button secondary" href="#signal-lab">Check your startup signals</a>
</section>
</div>
</div>

<section class="academy-quiz" id="academy-quiz">
<div class="quiz-heading">
<div><span>Final checkpoint</span><h3>Can you help Nessie launch a startup?</h3><p>Answer all ten questions. You’ll get a score, explanations, and the lessons worth reviewing.</p></div>
<img src="assets/images/nessie-mascot.png" alt="Nessie cheering you on">
</div>
<form id="startup-quiz">
<fieldset data-quiz-question="q1">
<legend><span>01</span>Which problem statement is most testable?</legend>
<label><input type="radio" name="q1" value="a"> Students need a better app.</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="q1" value="b"> Commuter students miss evening campus events because details are spread across several channels.</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="q1" value="c"> Everyone dislikes confusing technology.</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="q1" value="d"> College students report difficulty discovering events, so one calendar should combine every campus feed.</label>
<p class="quiz-explanation"></p>
</fieldset>
<fieldset data-quiz-question="q2">
<legend><span>02</span>What best defines a useful early customer segment?</legend>
<label><input type="radio" name="q2" value="a"> Anyone who might someday use the product</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="q2" value="b"> People of roughly the same age</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="q2" value="c"> A reachable group with a similar problem trigger, behavior, priority, and buying situation</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="q2" value="d"> People who follow startup accounts and say they like the idea</label>
<p class="quiz-explanation"></p>
</fieldset>
<fieldset data-quiz-question="q3">
<legend><span>03</span>What is an MVP primarily designed to do?</legend>
<label><input type="radio" name="q3" value="a"> Test the riskiest assumption with the smallest credible value experience</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="q3" value="b"> Include every feature competitors offer</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="q3" value="c"> Impress investors with polished code</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="q3" value="d"> Ship the smallest feature set the engineering team can finish in one sprint</label>
<p class="quiz-explanation"></p>
</fieldset>
<fieldset data-quiz-question="q4">
<legend><span>04</span>Which interview question produces the strongest evidence?</legend>
<label><input type="radio" name="q4" value="a"> Would you buy my idea?</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="q4" value="b"> Don’t you think this feature is useful?</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="q4" value="c"> Tell me about the last time this problem happened and what you did next.</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="q4" value="d"> After seeing this prototype, rank the three features you would be most likely to use.</label>
<p class="quiz-explanation"></p>
</fieldset>
<fieldset data-quiz-question="q5">
<legend><span>05</span>Which statement about TAM, SAM, and SOM is accurate?</legend>
<label><input type="radio" name="q5" value="a"> TAM is a guaranteed revenue forecast.</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="q5" value="b"> SOM is the realistic early share of the market you can actually serve.</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="q5" value="c"> SAM should always equal TAM.</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="q5" value="d"> SAM is the percentage of the serviceable market the startup expects to capture first.</label>
<p class="quiz-explanation"></p>
</fieldset>
<fieldset data-quiz-question="q6">
<legend><span>06</span>What makes a UVP useful?</legend>
<label><input type="radio" name="q6" value="a"> It names the customer, desired outcome, category, and credible difference.</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="q6" value="b"> It contains as many product features as possible.</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="q6" value="c"> It uses a clever slogan without mentioning value.</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="q6" value="d"> It states the primary benefit and promises the lowest price in the category.</label>
<p class="quiz-explanation"></p>
</fieldset>
<fieldset data-quiz-question="q7">
<legend><span>07</span>A social-media ad uses a paid creator. What should the startup do?</legend>
<label><input type="radio" name="q7" value="a"> Hide the relationship so the post feels organic.</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="q7" value="b"> Disclose the material connection clearly and support all advertising claims.</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="q7" value="c"> Ask the creator to guarantee results.</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="q7" value="d"> Put one general partnership disclosure in the creator’s profile biography.</label>
<p class="quiz-explanation"></p>
</fieldset>
<fieldset data-quiz-question="q8">
<legend><span>08</span>A unit sells for &#36;20 and has &#36;8 in direct COGS. What is its gross margin?</legend>
<label><input type="radio" name="q8" value="a"> 40%</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="q8" value="b"> 60%</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="q8" value="c"> 150%</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="q8" value="d"> It cannot be calculated without monthly fixed costs.</label>
<p class="quiz-explanation"></p>
</fieldset>
<fieldset data-quiz-question="q9">
<legend><span>09</span>Which statement correctly separates common IP types?</legend>
<label><input type="radio" name="q9" value="a"> A domain registration automatically creates a federal trademark.</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="q9" value="b"> A patent protects every business idea forever.</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="q9" value="c"> Trademarks identify source, patents may protect qualifying inventions, and copyright protects original expression.</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="q9" value="d"> Copyright protects a business name as soon as it is written in a brand guide.</label>
<p class="quiz-explanation"></p>
</fieldset>
<fieldset data-quiz-question="q10">
<legend><span>10</span>Which website launch practice is strongest?</legend>
<label><input type="radio" name="q10" value="a"> Document domain ownership, enable MFA and HTTPS, test accessibility/forms, and plan renewals and backups.</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="q10" value="b"> Buy a domain and assume hosting, email, security, and renewal happen automatically.</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="q10" value="c"> Collect every possible visitor detail in case it becomes useful.</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="q10" value="d"> Launch the site first, then add accessibility, security, policies, and ownership documentation after traction.</label>
<p class="quiz-explanation"></p>
</fieldset>
<div class="quiz-actions">

## Problem to solution

<div class="split-panel">
<div>
<span class="card-kicker">Problem statement</span>
<h3>Make the problem narrow enough to test</h3>
<p class="formula">[Specific user] struggles to [make progress] when [situation] because [root cause], which leads to [measurable cost].</p>
<p>“Students need a productivity app” is broad. “First-year commuters miss campus events because information is scattered across five channels” is testable.</p>
</div>
<div>
<span class="card-kicker">Solution hypothesis</span>
<h3>Describe an outcome, not a feature pile</h3>
<p class="formula">We believe [solution] will help [user] achieve [outcome]. We will know when [behavior or metric] changes.</p>
<p>Your first solution is a hypothesis. Learning that it is wrong early is progress, not failure.</p>
</div>
</div>

<div class="idea-canvas">
<div class="canvas-fields">
<span class="card-kicker">Your working notes</span>
<h3>Build a one-page idea canvas</h3>
<div class="canvas-field"><label for="canvas-user">Who are you helping?</label><input class="canvas-input" id="canvas-user" type="text" placeholder="Example: first-year commuter students"></div>
<div class="canvas-field"><label for="canvas-problem">What repeated problem do they face?</label><textarea class="canvas-input" id="canvas-problem" rows="3" placeholder="Describe a specific moment, not a broad topic"></textarea></div>
<div class="canvas-field"><label for="canvas-workaround">What do they use now?</label><input class="canvas-input" id="canvas-workaround" type="text" placeholder="Current workaround or alternative"></div>
<div class="canvas-field"><label for="canvas-test">What is the smallest test?</label><input class="canvas-input" id="canvas-test" type="text" placeholder="Interview, landing page, pilot, preorder…"></div>
</div>
<div class="canvas-preview">
<span class="card-kicker">Live draft</span>
<p id="canvas-preview-text">Start typing to turn your notes into a testable startup hypothesis.</p>
<button id="brainstorm-prompt" type="button">Shuffle a brainstorm prompt</button>
<div id="brainstorm-result">What expensive or annoying task does your campus still handle manually?</div>
<small>Your notes are saved only in this browser.</small>
</div>
</div>

</div>

## Ideas and brainstorming

<p class="section-intro">Strong startup ideas usually come from close observation: inconvenient workflows, excluded users, expensive delays, new technology, or a process you understand unusually well.</p>

<div class="card-grid four">
<article class="learning-card"><span class="card-kicker">Observe</span><h3>Keep a friction log</h3><p>Record repeated complaints, awkward workarounds, waiting, waste, and tasks people avoid.</p></article>
<article class="learning-card"><span class="card-kicker">Reframe</span><h3>Ask “How might we?”</h3><p>Turn a complaint into an open challenge without deciding the answer too early.</p></article>
<article class="learning-card"><span class="card-kicker">Expand</span><h3>Create 20 options</h3><p>Separate idea generation from judgment. Include manual, service, software, and community solutions.</p></article>
<article class="learning-card"><span class="card-kicker">Narrow</span><h3>Score the evidence</h3><p>Rank urgency, access to users, willingness to act, testability, and your unfair insight.</p></article>
</div>

<div class="prompt-box">
<strong>15-minute idea sprint</strong>
<p>Choose one community you know. List five repeated problems, three current workarounds for each, and one way to test demand this week for the strongest problem.</p>
</div>

## Validation and MVP

<div class="split-panel">
<div>
<span class="card-kicker">Customer discovery</span>
<h3>Interview the past, not the imaginary future</h3>
<ul class="mini-list">
<li>“Tell me about the last time this happened.”</li>
<li>“What did you do instead?”</li>
<li>“What did that cost in time, money, or stress?”</li>
<li>“Who decides whether to try or buy a solution?”</li>
</ul>
<p>Avoid pitching during discovery. The goal is to understand behavior and decision-making.</p>
</div>
<div>
<span class="card-kicker">Minimum viable product</span>
<h3>Build the smallest credible test</h3>
<ul class="mini-list">
<li>Clickable prototype for usability</li>
<li>Landing page or waitlist for demand</li>
<li>Manual concierge service for delivery</li>
<li>Paid pilot or preorder for willingness to pay</li>
</ul>
<p>An MVP is a learning instrument. Choose it based on the riskiest assumption—not the most exciting feature.</p>
</div>
</div>

<div class="resource-band">
<div><strong>Evidence before scale</strong><span>The NSF I-Corps program uses experiential customer discovery to reduce commercialization risk.</span></div>
<a href="https://www.nsf.gov/funding/initiatives/i-corps" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Explore NSF I-Corps ↗</a>
</div>

## Legal basics

<div class="legal-note"><strong>Educational guidance, not legal advice.</strong> Requirements depend on your country, state, industry, team, and customers. Use official sources and consult a qualified attorney or accountant for decisions with legal or tax consequences.</div>

<div class="card-grid three">
<article class="learning-card"><span class="card-kicker">Founders</span><h3>Put agreements in writing</h3><p>Clarify roles, ownership, vesting, decision rights, departures, and who owns work created for the startup.</p></article>
<article class="learning-card"><span class="card-kicker">Entity</span><h3>Choose structure deliberately</h3><p>Structure affects taxes, liability, paperwork, fundraising, and ownership. Do not copy another startup blindly.</p><a class="resource-link" href="https://www.sba.gov/business-guide/launch-your-business/choose-business-structure" target="_blank" rel="noopener">SBA structure guide ↗</a></article>
<article class="learning-card"><span class="card-kicker">Identity</span><h3>Check names and IP</h3><p>A domain or social handle does not establish trademark rights. Search similar marks and understand what your brand identifies.</p><a class="resource-link" href="https://www.uspto.gov/trademarks/basics" target="_blank" rel="noopener">USPTO trademark basics ↗</a></article>
<article class="learning-card"><span class="card-kicker">Registration</span><h3>Register in the right order</h3><p>Check state or local formation, licenses, permits, tax registration, and banking requirements. In the U.S., form an entity before requesting its EIN.</p><a class="resource-link" href="https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/get-an-employer-identification-number" target="_blank" rel="noopener">IRS EIN guidance ↗</a></article>
<article class="learning-card"><span class="card-kicker">Data</span><h3>Protect customer information</h3><p>Collect only what you need, secure access, explain usage clearly, and review rules for minors, health, education, payments, and location data.</p></article>
<article class="learning-card"><span class="card-kicker">People</span><h3>Know who works for you</h3><p>Employee and contractor classifications have different tax, wage, benefit, and IP consequences.</p></article>
</div>

## Financial foundations

<p class="section-intro">You do not need an MBA to understand startup finance. You do need a clear view of cash, costs, price, unit economics, and how long you can keep learning.</p>

<div class="card-grid four">
<article class="learning-card"><span class="card-kicker">Costs</span><h3>Separate one-time and monthly costs</h3><p>Include software, equipment, licenses, insurance, contractors, marketing, payment fees, and a realistic buffer.</p></article>
<article class="learning-card"><span class="card-kicker">Price</span><h3>Connect price to value</h3><p>Test willingness to pay. Revenue is stronger evidence than sign-ups, and margin matters more than revenue alone.</p></article>
<article class="learning-card"><span class="card-kicker">Cash</span><h3>Track burn and runway</h3><p>Net burn is monthly cash out minus cash in. Runway estimates how many months remain at the current burn.</p></article>
<article class="learning-card"><span class="card-kicker">Funding</span><h3>Match money to the milestone</h3><p>Bootstrapping, grants, competitions, loans, and equity each change risk, control, and expectations.</p></article>
</div>

<div class="resource-band">
<div><strong>Build a realistic cost map</strong><span>The SBA recommends identifying one-time and monthly expenses before launch, then using them for profit, break-even, and funding estimates.</span></div>
<a href="https://www.sba.gov/business-guide/plan-your-business/calculate-your-startup-costs" target="_blank" rel="noopener">SBA startup-cost guide ↗</a>
</div>

<div class="prediction-note">
<strong>What can you responsibly estimate?</strong>
<p>With consistent historical data, models can estimate retention risk, demand, revenue ranges, churn, cash runway, or a defined success score. They cannot know whether a startup will “succeed overall” with certainty. Predictions inherit the assumptions, missing information, and bias in their training data.</p>
</div>

```{r prepare-data, include=FALSE}

if (has_data) {
  dat <- raw |>
    transmute(
      startup_name = trimws(`Startup Name`),
      founded_year = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(`Founded Year`)),
      country = trimws(Country),
      industry = trimws(Industry),
      funding_stage = trimws(`Funding Stage`),
      total_funding_m = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(`Total Funding ($M)`)),
      employees = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(`Number of Employees`)),
      annual_revenue_m = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(`Annual Revenue ($M)`)),
      valuation_b = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(`Valuation ($B)`)),
      success_score = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(`Success Score`))
    ) |>
    filter(!is.na(success_score)) |>
    mutate(
      startup_age = pmax(as.integer(format(Sys.Date(), "%Y")) - founded_year, 0),
      across(c(country, industry, funding_stage), ~ na_if(.x, "")),
      across(c(country, industry, funding_stage), as.factor),
      # Log transforms reduce the leverage of unusually large startups.
      log_funding = log1p(pmax(total_funding_m, 0)),
      log_employees = log1p(pmax(employees, 0)),
      log_revenue = log1p(pmax(annual_revenue_m, 0)),
      log_valuation = log1p(pmax(valuation_b, 0))
    )

  if (nrow(dat) < 20) {
    stop("At least 20 rows with a numeric Success Score are needed; found ", nrow(dat), ".")
  }
  if (sd(dat$success_score, na.rm = TRUE) == 0) {
    stop("Success Score has no variation, so a regression cannot be estimated.")
  }

  quality <- tibble(
    variable = names(dat),
    type = vapply(dat, function(x) class(x)[1], character(1)),
    missing_n = vapply(dat, function(x) sum(is.na(x)), integer(1)),
    missing_pct = missing_n / nrow(dat),
    unique_n = vapply(dat, function(x) length(unique(x[!is.na(x)])), integer(1))
  )

}
```

## Research lab

<div class="research-banner">
<div><span class="card-kicker">R + LASSO</span><h3>Test startup signals with data</h3></div>
<p>The learning guides above help students make decisions today. This research lab asks a narrower question: which observed startup characteristics are associated with a defined <code>Success Score</code>?</p>
</div>

Two models are prepared. The earlier-stage model uses age, country, industry,
funding stage, total funding, and employee count. The all-observed model adds
annual revenue and valuation. Because revenue and valuation may be consequences
of success, the second model is descriptive rather than causal.

### Dataset overview

The dashboard begins with a basic data-quality check before showing any model
results. Missing values, sample size, and category coverage matter because a
clean-looking graph can still be misleading when the underlying sample is thin.

```{r quality-table}
  knitr::kable(
    quality,
    digits = 3,
    col.names = c("Variable", "Type", "Missing", "Missing %", "Unique values"),
    caption = paste("Data quality summary for", nrow(dat), "usable startups")
  )
}
```

```{r overview, fig.height=4.5}
  summary_stats <- dat |>
    summarise(
      startups = n(),
```

### Factor comparisons

Pearson correlation measures linear association; Spearman correlation also detects
monotonic relationships and is less sensitive to extreme values. Correlation does
not establish that a factor causes startup success.

```{r correlations}
if (has_data) {
  numeric_for_cor <- dat |>
    select(
      success_score, founded_year, startup_age, total_funding_m,
      employees, annual_revenue_m, valuation_b
    )

  target_correlations <- setdiff(names(numeric_for_cor), "success_score") |>
    lapply(function(v) {
      complete <- complete.cases(numeric_for_cor[[v]], numeric_for_cor$success_score)
      tibble(
        factor = v,
        complete_n = sum(complete),
        pearson = if (sum(complete) >= 3)
          cor(numeric_for_cor[[v]][complete],
              numeric_for_cor$success_score[complete], method = "pearson") else NA_real_,
        spearman = if (sum(complete) >= 3)
          cor(numeric_for_cor[[v]][complete],
              numeric_for_cor$success_score[complete], method = "spearman") else NA_real_
      )
    }) |>
    bind_rows() |>
    arrange(desc(abs(spearman)))

  knitr::kable(
    target_correlations, digits = 3,
    col.names = c("Factor", "Complete N", "Pearson r", "Spearman rho"),
    caption = "Bivariate associations with Success Score"
  )
}
```

```{r numeric-plots, fig.height=7}
if (has_data) {
  relationship_data <- dat |>
    select(
      success_score, `Startup age` = startup_age,
      `Total funding ($M)` = total_funding_m,
      Employees = employees,
      `Annual revenue ($M)` = annual_revenue_m,
      `Valuation ($B)` = valuation_b
    ) |>
    pivot_longer(-success_score, names_to = "factor", values_to = "value")

  ggplot(relationship_data, aes(value, success_score)) +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.5, color = launch_palette$teal) +
    geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, color = launch_palette$sage, linewidth = 0.7) +
    facet_wrap(~ factor, scales = "free_x", ncol = 2) +
    labs(
      title = "Numeric factors and startup success",
      subtitle = "Lines show separate unadjusted linear relationships",
      x = NULL, y = "Success score"
    )
}
```

#### Country, industry, and funding-stage relationships

Group averages can be unstable for categories represented by few startups.
Accordingly, each plot shows the group sample size and only displays the 12
largest groups.

```{r grouped-relations, fig.height=10}
if (has_data) {
  group_summary <- function(data, variable) {
    data |>
      filter(!is.na(.data[[variable]])) |>
      group_by(group = .data[[variable]]) |>
      summarise(
        n = n(),
        mean_success = mean(success_score, na.rm = TRUE),
        se = sd(success_score, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(n),
        .groups = "drop"
      ) |>
      slice_max(n, n = 12, with_ties = FALSE) |>
      mutate(
        lower = mean_success - 1.96 * se,
        upper = mean_success + 1.96 * se,
        group = reorder(paste0(group, " (n=", n, ")"), mean_success)
      )
  }

  group_plot <- function(summary_data, title) {
    ggplot(summary_data, aes(mean_success, group)) +
      geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = lower, xmax = upper), height = 0.15, color = launch_palette$mauve) +
      geom_point(size = 2.4, color = launch_palette$teal) +
      labs(title = title, x = "Mean success score (95% interval)", y = NULL)
  }

  print(group_plot(group_summary(dat, "funding_stage"), "Success by funding stage"))
  print(group_plot(group_summary(dat, "industry"), "Success by industry"))
  print(group_plot(group_summary(dat, "country"), "Success by country"))
}
```

### LASSO regression

The data are split 80/20 into training and test sets. All imputation, dummy
encoding, removal of zero-variance columns, and standardization are learned only
from the training data. Cross-validation selects the penalty. The conservative
`lambda.1se` value is used for the final model; it usually produces a smaller,
more stable set of predictors than the minimum-error penalty.

```{r lasso-functions}
if (has_data) {
  set.seed(params$seed)
  train_ids <- sample(seq_len(nrow(dat)), size = floor(0.80 * nrow(dat)))
  train <- dat[train_ids, , drop = FALSE]
  test <- dat[-train_ids, , drop = FALSE]

  run_lasso <- function(train, test, predictors, model_name) {
    model_formula <- reformulate(predictors, response = "success_score")

    rec <- recipe(model_formula, data = train) |>
      step_unknown(all_nominal_predictors(), new_level = "Unknown") |>
      step_novel(all_nominal_predictors(), new_level = "New") |>
      step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) |>
      step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors(), one_hot = TRUE) |>
      step_zv(all_predictors()) |>
      step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())

    trained_recipe <- prep(rec, training = train, retain = TRUE)
    train_baked <- bake(trained_recipe, new_data = train)
    test_baked <- bake(trained_recipe, new_data = test)

    x_train <- as.matrix(select(train_baked, -success_score))
    y_train <- train_baked$success_score
    x_test <- as.matrix(select(test_baked, -success_score))
    y_test <- test_baked$success_score

    set.seed(params$seed)
    folds <- min(10, max(3, floor(nrow(x_train) / 5)))
    cv_fit <- cv.glmnet(
      x_train, y_train,
      alpha = 1,
      family = "gaussian",
      nfolds = folds,
      standardize = FALSE,
      type.measure = "mse"
    )

    predictions <- as.numeric(
      predict(cv_fit, newx = x_test, s = "lambda.1se")
    )
    baseline <- rep(mean(y_train), length(y_test))
    test_sse <- sum((y_test - predictions)^2)
    test_sst <- sum((y_test - mean(y_test))^2)

    metrics <- tibble(
      model = model_name,
      test_n = length(y_test),
      selected_predictors =
        sum(as.matrix(coef(cv_fit, s = "lambda.1se"))[-1, 1] != 0),
      lambda = cv_fit$lambda.1se,
      rmse = sqrt(mean((y_test - predictions)^2)),
      mae = mean(abs(y_test - predictions)),
      r_squared = if (test_sst > 0) 1 - test_sse / test_sst else NA_real_,
      baseline_rmse = sqrt(mean((y_test - baseline)^2))
    )

    coefficient_matrix <- as.matrix(coef(cv_fit, s = "lambda.1se"))
    coefficients <- tibble(
      factor = rownames(coefficient_matrix),
      coefficient = as.numeric(coefficient_matrix[, 1])
    ) |>
      filter(factor != "(Intercept)", coefficient != 0) |>
      mutate(abs_coefficient = abs(coefficient)) |>
      arrange(desc(abs_coefficient))

    predictions_table <- tibble(
      actual = y_test,
      predicted = predictions,
      residual = y_test - predictions
    )

    list(
      recipe = trained_recipe,
      fit = cv_fit,
      metrics = metrics,
      coefficients = coefficients,
      predictions = predictions_table
    )
  }

  early_predictors <- c(
    "startup_age", "country", "industry", "funding_stage",
    "log_funding", "log_employees"
  )
  all_predictors <- c(
    early_predictors, "log_revenue", "log_valuation"
  )

  early_lasso <- run_lasso(train, test, early_predictors, "Earlier-stage factors")
  all_lasso <- run_lasso(train, test, all_predictors, "All observed factors")
}
```

#### Out-of-sample performance

```{r model-performance}
if (has_data) {
  performance <- bind_rows(early_lasso$metrics, all_lasso$metrics)
  knitr::kable(
    performance, digits = 3,
    col.names = c(
      "Model", "Test N", "Selected", "Lambda", "RMSE", "MAE",
      "Test R-squared", "Mean-only RMSE"
    )
  )
}
```

A useful model should have RMSE below the mean-only baseline on held-out data.
Negative test R-squared means the model generalized worse than simply predicting
the test-set mean.

#### Selected factors

Because inputs are standardized, coefficient magnitudes are broadly comparable.
A positive coefficient is associated with a higher predicted success score,
holding the other included variables constant; a zero coefficient was excluded
by LASSO. Category coefficients are relative to the omitted reference category.

```{r selected-coefficients, fig.height=8}
if (has_data) {
  selected <- bind_rows(
    mutate(early_lasso$coefficients, model = "Earlier-stage factors"),
    mutate(all_lasso$coefficients, model = "All observed factors")
  )

  if (nrow(selected) == 0) {
    cat("At the conservative lambda.1se penalty, LASSO selected no predictors.")
  } else {
    print(
      knitr::kable(
        selected |>
          group_by(model) |>
          slice_max(abs_coefficient, n = 20, with_ties = FALSE) |>
          ungroup() |>
          select(model, factor, coefficient),
        digits = 3,
        col.names = c("Model", "Selected factor", "Standardized coefficient")
      )
    )

    selected |>
      group_by(model) |>
      slice_max(abs_coefficient, n = 15, with_ties = FALSE) |>
      ungroup() |>
      mutate(
        factor = reorder(factor, coefficient),
        direction = if_else(coefficient > 0, "Positive", "Negative")
      ) |>
      ggplot(aes(coefficient, factor, fill = direction)) +
      geom_col() +
      facet_wrap(~ model, scales = "free_y") +
      scale_fill_manual(values = c(
        Positive = launch_palette$teal,
        Negative = launch_palette$mauve
      )) +
      labs(
        title = "Strongest factors retained by LASSO",
        subtitle = "Standardized coefficients at the one-standard-error penalty",
        x = "Coefficient", y = NULL, fill = "Association"
      )
  }
}
```

#### Prediction check

```{r prediction-check, fig.height=4.8}
if (has_data) {
  prediction_plot_data <- bind_rows(
    mutate(early_lasso$predictions, model = "Earlier-stage factors"),
    mutate(all_lasso$predictions, model = "All observed factors")
  )

  ggplot(prediction_plot_data, aes(actual, predicted)) +
    geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = 2, color = launch_palette$mauve) +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.7, color = launch_palette$teal) +
    facet_wrap(~ model) +
    coord_equal() +
    labs(
      title = "Held-out predictions versus actual scores",
      subtitle = "Points closer to the dashed 45-degree line are more accurate",
      x = "Actual success score", y = "Predicted success score"
    )
}
```

### Research conclusions

- These results identify **associations**, not causal effects. Funding, hiring,
  revenue, valuation, and success may influence one another.
- The startup name is excluded because it is an identifier, not a reusable
  explanatory factor.
- LASSO may choose one variable from a group of highly correlated variables and
  shrink the others to zero. A zero coefficient does not prove that a factor is
  irrelevant.
- Country and industry estimates need adequate representation. Results for small
  categories are unstable and should not drive decisions alone.
- The held-out test metrics are the best guide to whether the relationships
  generalize beyond this sample.
- A stronger causal analysis would require time-stamped predictors measured before
  the success outcome, a clear definition of `Success Score`, and preferably
  repeated observations over time.

### Research methodology

The analysis uses an 80/20 training-test split. Preprocessing is learned from the
training data only: missing numeric values are median-imputed, new and missing
categories are handled explicitly, categorical variables are dummy encoded, and
numeric predictors are standardized. Ten-fold cross-validation (or fewer folds
for small samples) selects the LASSO penalty. The conservative one-standard-error
penalty is reported to favor a simpler model.

The full R source is available in the project repository so every figure and
metric can be rebuilt when the dataset changes.
